passage:
"I can't do it, Saurabh. I'm quitting the swimming class."
Her husband looked up from the laptop. "What happened?"
"Everyone else floated by week three. I still sink like a stone. I'm twenty-five, I'm too old, I just can't swim."
"Can't, or can't yet?"
Sonali threw a wet towel at him. "Don't do the poster thing."
"I'm not. Just... what have you tried?"
She sat down, dripping. "Kicking harder. It makes it worse."
"So kicking harder isn't it. What else is there?"
A pause. "The coach said something about breathing out slowly and keeping my head down. I kept lifting it to look."
"So try that on Saturday?"
"Fine." She wrung out her hair. "I can't float. Yet." She said the last word as if she didn't quite trust it. "And I'll ask the coach to watch my head."

qa.q: What did the coach say about breathing and her head?
qa.a: Breathing out slowly and keeping her head down.

qa.q: What is Sonali feeling when she says 'Yet' as if she doesn't quite trust it?
qa.a: Still frustrated and doubtful, but opening a door; she half-believes progress is possible and is willing to test it.

qa.q: What turning point in the conversation helped Sonali plan her next try?
qa.a: Saurabh asking what she had tried; seeing that kicking harder made it worse led her to a new strategy, breathing out and head down, with the coach watching.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel when the towel comes flying?
qa.a: Saurabh probably takes it with good humour 😄, understands her frustration, and chooses questions over slogans so she doesn't feel lectured.

grounding: An adult turns 'I can't swim' into 'I can't yet' and pairs it with a new strategy to try next.

passage: When I moved to Bengaluru for my first nursing job, I told everyone, "I can't speak Kannada. I'm hopeless with languages." I'm Beena, from Kottayam. For three months I pointed and smiled at patients' families and felt useless. My friend Kiranjit, a Punjabi who'd learned Tamil in Chennai, said, "You mean you can't yet." I rolled my eyes. But the word stuck. Then she asked, "What have you actually tried?" Honestly, just a phrasebook I never opened. So I changed the plan: five ward phrases a week, written on my palm, used with real patients, and the night-shift attendant correcting me. Four months later I can explain the meal times and ask where it hurts. Plenty still goes over my head. But "I can't" has become "not yet, and here are next week's five."

qa.q: How many ward phrases did Beena learn each week?
qa.a: Five ward phrases a week.

qa.q: Why did Beena feel useless in the first three months?
qa.a: Without Kannada, Beena could only point and smile instead of really helping families, and 'I'm hopeless with languages' made the gap feel permanent.

qa.q: What choice turned 'yet' into real progress for Beena?
qa.a: Swapping the unopened phrasebook for five phrases a week, used on the ward and corrected by the night-shift attendant; the word opened the door and the method did the work.

qa.q: How might patients' families experience the change in Beena?
qa.a: They can now hear the meal times and be asked where it hurts in their own language, which likely makes them feel more cared for and less anxious.

grounding: An adult replaces 'I can't speak the language' with 'not yet' and backs it with a concrete weekly method.

passage:
Week one: Vidya, newly promoted to lead the loan-processing team, pinned up a poster: "Mistakes are how we grow." In the Monday meeting she told everyone to stretch themselves. Raghav, the youngest analyst, nodded and said nothing.
Week three: Raghav made an error on a new type of file. The regional head copied the whole floor on an angry email. Raghav stayed at his desk through lunch, face grey. Vidya noticed that nobody volunteered for the new file types after that.
Week six: Vidya took the poster down. She blocked two hours every Friday for learning new files, paired Raghav with a senior, and asked the regional head to send corrections to her privately. By the next month, three people had asked to try the complex files.

qa.q: What did the poster Vidya pinned up say?
qa.a: 'Mistakes are how we grow.'

qa.q: What did the team likely feel after the angry email, and what shows it?
qa.a: Afraid of being shamed in public; Raghav's grey face and the sudden lack of volunteers show that the poster's words didn't feel safe to believe.

qa.q: What changes did Vidya make in week six, and why did they work better than the poster?
qa.a: Two protected hours on Fridays, pairing with a senior, and private corrections; these gave time, feedback and safety, so learning became possible.

qa.q: How might Raghav experience the Friday pairing compared with week three?
qa.a: Instead of being exposed in front of the whole floor, Raghav gets time and a senior's help, so mistakes feel like part of learning rather than a threat.

grounding: A manager sees that growth slogans fail without time, feedback and safety, and changes the conditions instead.

passage: Nandini, you've just become a manager and you're printing "growth mindset" posters? Sit a minute. When I was twenty-six, I ran a small team at a textile mill's quality lab in Coimbatore. I'd read a book about believing you can grow, and I made everyone repeat it. "Challenges are chances!" Meanwhile the lab ran twelve-hour shifts, nobody got feedback except shouting, and a girl who asked a question was mocked for weeks. Of course nobody grew. They were too busy surviving. What changed things wasn't my speeches. It was half an hour every Thursday, while the machines were serviced, when I sat with one person and went through their tests, and a rule that nobody laughed at questions. I'm Farida, and I learned it late: belief needs somewhere to live.

qa.q: How long were the shifts in Farida's lab?
qa.a: The lab ran twelve-hour shifts.

qa.q: Why were the speeches not enough, in Farida's view?
qa.a: Farida saw that the team felt exhausted and afraid, surviving long shifts, shouting and mockery, so words about growing had nothing to stand on.

qa.q: What choices finally made growth possible in Farida's lab?
qa.a: Half an hour each Thursday going through one person's tests, and a rule that nobody laughed at questions; time, feedback and safety gave the belief somewhere to live.

qa.q: How might Nandini's new team feel about posters without that kind of support?
qa.a: They might roll their eyes or feel pressured, hearing 'grow' while lacking the time and safety to try, much like Farida's lab once did.

grounding: An elder recalls learning, as a young manager, that growth talk fails without time, feedback and safety to learn.

subtype: Feeling like a fraud in a top college [Actor]
passage:
Wednesday, hostel, 1 a.m.
First quiz back. 14 out of 20. Payal got 19. Payal also finished the lab in forty minutes while I was still reading the instructions.
Everyone here was a topper somewhere. I only got in because the entrance paper that year was full of the chapters I'd revised twice. That's luck, not brains. Any day now someone will look at my file and say, "Wait, how is SHE here?"
Amma called and said, "You cleared an exam lakhs of people wrote." She doesn't get it. Clearing it doesn't count if it was the easy year.
14 is above the class average, apparently. It doesn't feel like it. It feels like a warning.
- Indu

qa.q: What did Indu score on the first quiz?
qa.a: 14 out of 20.

qa.q: Why does 14 out of 20 feel like a warning to Indu?
qa.a: Indu feels anxious, comparing only with Payal's 19 and believing the admission was luck, so even an above-average mark seems like evidence she'll be found out.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Indu judged the quiz, and what could help?
qa.a: Indu dismissed her own success and compared harshly with one classmate; noting facts, like being above average and clearing an exam lakhs wrote, could balance the story.

qa.q: How might Amma feel when Indu brushes off her words?
qa.a: Amma may feel proud but helpless, sensing her daughter can't take in an achievement Amma sees so clearly.

grounding: A student at a top institute believes she got in by luck, discounts an above-average mark and compares harshly.

passage:
"Nitin, you've been quiet since you came home. College okay?"
"Fine, Bhabhi." Nitin pushed the rice around the plate.
Hafsa sat down across the table. "Your brother says you topped the first test."
"I did. But in class they talk about moots and internships and 'chambers', and I don't know what half of it means. Everyone's father is a lawyer. They all know the rules."
"And you think that means you don't belong?"
"I think it means I'm faking it."
Hafsa was quiet for a moment. "When I started nursing college, I didn't know what a viva was. I thought it was a test you could fail for being poor." She laughed. "It's just words, Nitin. You're learning the words. You already have the marks."
"There's a first-generation students' group. I saw a poster."
"Then go on Friday. Take someone from your bench."

qa.q: What did Nitin top?
qa.a: Nitin topped the first test.

qa.q: Why does Nitin feel like a fake despite topping the test?
qa.a: Nitin feels out of place and insecure, because classmates use codes (moots, internships, chambers) their lawyer parents taught them, so Nitin reads not knowing the words as not belonging.

qa.q: What turning point does Hafsa offer, and what choice follows?
qa.a: Her story about not knowing what a viva was reframes the gap as unfamiliar words, not ability; Nitin then thinks about going to the first-generation group on Friday.

qa.q: Why might Hafsa share her own nursing-college story?
qa.a: Hafsa seems to want Nitin to see that the lost feeling is common and passes, and that she understands it from the inside.

grounding: A first-generation law student with top marks feels like a fake among classmates who know the codes, and family points to community.

passage: My first semester at the engineering college in Pune, I ate lunch alone most days. I'm Hrithik, the first in my family to study past Class 10; my father repairs pumps in Latur. I had good marks, but everything else was a foreign language: "office hours", "electives", emailing a professor. I assumed everyone could see I didn't belong. When I got an A in circuits, I thought the grader had been sloppy. Then Pankaj, a third-year from a small town near Solapur, sat down with his tray and said, "You're in my hostel wing, right? Nobody tells you what office hours are. I'll show you." He took me to a first-generation students' meet that Saturday. Twelve of us, all confused by the same things. The A, it turned out, was just an A.

qa.q: Where does Hrithik's father repair pumps?
qa.a: In Latur.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik think the grader had been sloppy?
qa.a: Feeling out of place made Hrithik distrust any sign of belonging, so even a good grade seemed like a mistake rather than proof of ability.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Pankaj explaining office hours and taking Hrithik to the first-generation meet; finding twelve others confused by the same codes showed the problem was unfamiliarity, not ability 🙂

qa.q: What might it mean to Pankaj to help Hrithik?
qa.a: Coming from a small town himself, Pankaj probably remembers the same confusion and is glad to spare someone else a lonely first semester.

grounding: A first-generation engineering student doubts belonging despite good marks until a senior and a peer group show it is unfamiliar codes, not ability.

subtype: Working overly hard to avoid exposure [Actor]
passage: Mridul, you asked why I'm never at the Friday dinners. Okay, the real reason. I joined the audit firm in June and I'm terrified they'll figure out I don't know enough. So I stay till ten every night. I prepare notes for meetings I'm not even invited to. I read every past file twice. Last month my manager said my report was the best from the new batch, and for about an hour I felt amazing. Relief, basically. Then I thought, that's only because I worked till midnight all week. If I ever stop, they'll see. So I worked till midnight the next week too. It's like proving it all over again every day, and it never sticks. I'm Eshaan, I'm tired, and I still don't believe I'm good at this.

qa.q: Until what time does Eshaan stay at the office every night?
qa.a: Eshaan stays till ten every night.

qa.q: Why doesn't the manager's praise last for Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan credits the good report to overwork, not ability, so the relief fades and the fear of exposure returns, demanding even more hours.

qa.q: What choice could break the cycle for Eshaan?
qa.a: Leaving on time for one week on a normal report and seeing how it's received; if it's still good, that is evidence the skill, not the overwork, carries the work.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel hearing 'I'm tired'?
qa.a: Mridul would likely feel worried and glad to be trusted with the truth, and may want to gently pull Eshaan back to the Friday dinners.

grounding: A new employee overworks out of fear of being seen as unqualified and credits every success to the extra hours.

subtype: Working overly hard to avoid exposure [Actor]
passage: I'm Farhan, and I sit opposite Ganga at the civil engineering firm. She joined in April, straight out of college. Her drawings are clean; her calculations rarely need checking. Yet she's the last to leave every night, lights off except her desk lamp. She brings three versions of every sketch to reviews, "just in case". When the director praised her bridge-load report, she said, "I just put in a lot of hours," and went straight back to work. One night I asked why she stayed so late. She laughed a bit too fast. "If I leave at six, someone will find the mistake I missed." I can't know everything she feels, but it looks as if the more she overworks, the more convinced she is that overwork is all she's got.

qa.q: How many versions of every sketch does Ganga bring to reviews?
qa.a: Three versions.

qa.q: What does Ganga's too-fast laugh suggest?
qa.a: She seems anxious and a little embarrassed, afraid that leaving at six would expose her, and uneasy admitting it.

qa.q: What could Farhan say or do that might help Ganga see her real skill?
qa.a: Point out specifically that her calculations rarely need checking and that the report was praised for its content, and suggest trying one review with a single version.

qa.q: How does Ganga's pattern look from Farhan's desk?
qa.a: To Farhan it looks like a trap: every success gets credited to the late hours, which only deepens her belief that overwork is all she has.

grounding: A colleague sees a capable new engineer over-prepare and stay late out of fear, crediting her success to overwork.

passage: For a year I didn't notice Mahima at all, and I'm a little ashamed of that. I'm Deepak, a product analyst at a payments startup in Gurugram. She sat in the corner during our weekly meetings, said nothing and took notes. Then I joined the payments project, and I saw that every clean dataset and every fixed bug traced back to her. When our lead offered her the team-lead role in March, she turned it down. "Someone who speaks better should do it," she said. After the meeting I went to her desk. "Mahima, your error checks saved us from a failed launch in January. You caught the currency bug nobody else saw. People come to you, not the lead, when they're stuck." She looked at me for a long moment, then said quietly, "I didn't know anyone noticed."

qa.q: Which bug did Mahima catch?
qa.a: The currency bug nobody else saw.

qa.q: What does Mahima's 'I didn't know anyone noticed' suggest about her?
qa.a: She has been quietly doubting her worth, assuming her contributions were invisible, which helps explain turning down the role.

qa.q: What did Deepak do well in speaking to Mahima?
qa.a: Deepak named specific contributions, the error checks, the currency bug, people coming to her, rather than vague praise, giving her facts that are hard to dismiss.

qa.q: How might Mahima see her own work after Deepak's words?
qa.a: She may start to see her quiet work as valuable and visible, which could change how she thinks about the next promotion.

grounding: A colleague notices a quiet, accomplished teammate who turns down promotion and tells her exactly what value she brings.

passage:
Note to myself before the team review, 2 May. Rehana, senior accountant.
Zainab has been on our team three years. In meetings she never speaks; she slides a printout across instead. Last week she turned down the audit lead role for the second time. "I'm not ready," she said, looking at the table. But I've seen her work closely. She rebuilt our reconciliation process last year, and month-end now takes three days instead of six. The juniors go to her, not me, when they're stuck. So today, after the meeting, I told her exactly that: the three days, the juniors, the tax query she solved in an hour that had stuck the rest of us for a week. She went quiet, then asked if she could think about the role over the weekend. I said yes. I'll raise it again at the review.

qa.q: How long does month-end take now?
qa.a: Month-end now takes three days instead of six.

qa.q: What might Zainab be feeling when she says 'I'm not ready' while looking at the table?
qa.a: She seems full of quiet doubt, underestimating herself despite clear results, and perhaps uneasy about being noticed at all.

qa.q: What choice did Rehana make after the meeting, and why might it matter?
qa.a: Rehana named specific results, the three-day month-end, the juniors, the tax query; concrete facts are harder to wave away than general encouragement.

qa.q: How might the juniors see Zainab possibly leading the audit?
qa.a: They already turn to her when stuck, so they would probably welcome it and feel more confident with her officially in charge 🙂

grounding: A senior colleague notices a quietly accomplished accountant who stays silent and refuses promotion, and names her specific value.

passage: I'm Francis, and I've been at the civil engineering firm for fifteen years. Samir joined our structures team last year, twenty-five and very sharp. A few weeks ago he stayed back after everyone left and said, "Can I tell you something stupid? I feel like a fraud. Any day someone will realise I don't really know load calculations." I told him the truth: in my second year I hid in the stairwell before every site review, sure I'd be found out. And our chief engineer once told me she still feels it before big presentations. Samir stared at me. "Even her?" "Even her." Since then I've noticed he asks questions in meetings instead of staying silent, and last week he joked about "fraud club" over tea. He seems lighter.

qa.q: Where did Francis hide before every site review?
qa.a: In the stairwell.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he asked, 'Can I tell you something stupid?'
qa.a: Ashamed and scared, expecting the fear to sound silly and half-expecting to be judged for saying it aloud.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Samir, and what changed after it?
qa.a: Hearing that Francis and the chief engineer felt the same; the shame eased, and Samir began asking questions in meetings and joking about 'fraud club'.

qa.q: What might sharing the stairwell story have cost and given Francis?
qa.a: It meant admitting an old weakness to a junior, but it let Francis help Samir feel less alone, and perhaps brought some relief in saying it too.

grounding: A senior colleague sees how confiding the feeling of being a fraud, and hearing it is common, lifts a young engineer's shame.

passage:
Monday: Noor, three months into her job as a junior editor at a publishing house, stayed late again, rereading a manuscript she'd already checked twice. When her boss praised her notes, she felt sick. They'll find out soon, she thought. She told no one.
Thursday: At lunch with Thomas, her old college mentor, she finally said it. "I think I'm a fraud. Everyone else seems to belong there." Thomas put down his fork. "Noor, I've edited for twenty years. I felt that for my first ten. So did half the people I've admired." She stared at him. "Really?" "Really. It's so common it has a name."
The next Tuesday: When her boss praised her again, the old fear flickered. But she wrote down what was praised, and went home at six.

qa.q: How long did Thomas say he felt like a fraud?
qa.a: He felt that for his first ten years.

qa.q: Why did Noor feel sick when her boss praised her notes on Monday?
qa.a: Noor felt afraid of being exposed: believing she was a fraud, she took the praise as raising the stakes of being found out rather than as a sign of her skill.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Noor do differently afterwards?
qa.a: Telling Thomas and hearing he felt the same for ten years; the next Tuesday she noted what was praised and went home at six instead of rechecking.

qa.q: What might Thomas feel as Noor shares this at lunch?
qa.a: Thomas might feel honoured she trusted him, and glad to offer the relief he may have wished for early in his own career.

grounding: An adult who confides feeling like a fraud to a mentor learns it is common, which eases her shame over the following days.

passage: At the parent-teacher meeting in the Class 5 room, Seema sat beside her father, Jomon, swinging her legs. The teacher smiled. "Seema's story about her grandmother's goat was the best in the class. And she's started helping the new girl with reading." Jomon nodded politely and turned the report card over. "And maths? Why only 42 out of 50?" The teacher began to answer. Seema's legs stopped swinging. She knew what came next: the quiet drive home, no bakery stop. In her bag was a spelling test with 7 out of 10 that she hadn't shown anyone. She pressed the bag shut with her foot. On the way out, her father squeezed her shoulder and said, "Next time, 50, okay?" She nodded. She wished he'd asked about the goat.

qa.q: What did the teacher say was the best in the class?
qa.a: Seema's story about her grandmother's goat.

qa.q: Why did Seema's legs stop swinging?
qa.a: She knew from experience that anything less than full marks meant a quiet drive home and no treat, so she felt her father's warmth slipping away.

qa.q: What could Jomon have done at the meeting to make Seema feel valued beyond marks?
qa.a: Responded first to the goat story and her kindness to the new girl, and asked about maths calmly, so she knows his affection doesn't hinge on 50.

qa.q: How might the teacher see the exchange?
qa.a: The teacher tried to share Seema's creativity and kindness and may notice both were brushed aside, perhaps worrying about the pressure Seema carries.

grounding: A child whose father responds only to marks hides a lower test and feels his warmth depends on full scores.

passage: I'm Zainab, Aditi's cousin; I stay with her family during college term. Last Friday Aditi came home from school, went straight to her room and slid something under her mattress. Later, making her bed, I found it: a science test, 13 out of 20, with "Good effort!" in green. At dinner Khala asked, "Any tests back?" Aditi said, "No." When she brought home 20 out of 20 last month, Khala hugged her, phoned the whole family and made kheer. When it's less, the room just goes quiet. That night Aditi whispered to me, "Ammi loves me more when I get full marks." I held her and said, "I love you with a 13. Your Ammi loves you with a 13 too." Tomorrow I'm going to tell Khala what she said.

qa.q: What score was on the test under the mattress?
qa.a: 13 out of 20.

qa.q: Why did Aditi hide the test and say 'No' at dinner?
qa.a: She believes her mother loves her more for full marks, so a 13 feels like a risk to that love and hiding it seems safer.

qa.q: What choice did Zainab make that night, and what comes next?
qa.a: Zainab held Aditi and said she is loved with a 13, and plans to tell Khala what Aditi said so the home can start noticing effort, not only full marks.

qa.q: How might Khala feel on learning that Aditi thinks love depends on marks?
qa.a: Khala would likely be shocked and hurt, since she probably meant the kheer as joy rather than a condition, and might want to show affection more evenly.

grounding: A cousin sees a child hide a lower mark because she feels her mother's love depends on full marks.

passage: In their Chennai flat, Keerthana had been on the first page of her English essay since seven. The opening line was never right. She wrote it, read it, rubbed it out. Wrote it again. By ten the top of the paper had worn thin and grey, and when she pressed the eraser once more, it tore. Her younger brother Sahil peeped in. "Akka, it's due tomorrow. Just write the rest." "I can't write the rest if the start is wrong." "Your last essay got 18 out of 20." "That's why this one can't be worse." She took a fresh sheet. The clock ticked past eleven. In the morning she handed in nothing and told the teacher she'd left it at home. It felt safer than a page that wasn't perfect.

qa.q: What happened when Keerthana pressed the eraser once more?
qa.a: The paper tore.

qa.q: Why did handing in nothing feel safer to Keerthana?
qa.a: With the bar set at her last 18 or better, any imperfect page felt like failing, so not finishing avoided being judged.

qa.q: What small step could Keerthana try next time the opening won't come right?
qa.a: Leave a rough first line and write the rest, then come back to it; a messy draft that exists can be improved, but a blank page can't.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel watching his sister erase until the paper tore?
qa.a: Sahil might be puzzled and worried, seeing that the problem isn't ability, since her last essay got 18, but a fear he can't talk her out of.

grounding: A teenager rewrites the opening of an essay until the paper tears and hands in nothing because finishing imperfectly feels like failing.

passage:
"Urmila, why is the bin full of chart paper?"
"It's the science poster, Papa. It keeps going wrong."
Her father, Darshan, pulled out a sheet. "This looks good. What's wrong with it?"
"The title's not centred. And on the next one the arrow's crooked."
"How many sheets have you used?"
"Seven."
"When is it due?"
"Tomorrow." Her voice cracked. "If it isn't perfect, it's not worth giving. Ma'am will put it on the wall with everyone else's."
Darshan sat on the floor beside her. "So right now you have zero posters and seven nearly good ones."
"Nearly isn't good."
"Pick the least-bad one. Finish it in one hour, crooked arrow and all. Then dinner."
Urmila stared at the pile. "What if it's ugly?"
"Then it's a finished ugly poster. That beats an empty space on the wall."

qa.q: How many sheets had Urmila used?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: What does 'Nearly isn't good' show about Urmila's thinking?
qa.a: Her standard is so high that anything short of perfect counts as failure, so finishing a flawed poster feels worse than having none.

qa.q: What choice does Darshan suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Picking the least-bad sheet and finishing it within an hour; a time limit and permission to be imperfect turn endless redoing into something handed in.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel seeing seven good-looking sheets in the bin?
qa.a: Darshan is probably surprised and concerned, since the work looks good to him, and realises the problem is her fear of imperfection, not her skill.

grounding: A teenager restarts a poster seven times because none is perfect and risks handing in nothing, until her father sets a limit.

passage:
Sunday, 2 a.m.
Fourth draft of the history seminar paper. Neelam finished hers on Friday and went to the movies. I couldn't. Every paragraph has to be the kind that makes Professor Rao say "excellent" like he did in first year. Since then I've been "the one who never makes mistakes". They say it at home too.
The truth, which I only write here: I'm not sure I even like history anymore. I like not being caught. If one footnote is wrong, everyone will see I'm ordinary, just a normal student who got lucky with praise.
Neelam messaged: "Don't you enjoy it at all?" I didn't answer. I used to. In school I read about the Cholas for fun, under the blanket with a torch.
Maybe I can find that again.
- Gargi

qa.q: What did Neelam do after finishing on Friday?
qa.a: Neelam went to the movies.

qa.q: What does Gargi seem to feel is really driving the fourth draft?
qa.a: Fear more than love: Gargi writes that the real goal is 'not being caught', dreading that one wrong footnote will reveal someone ordinary.

qa.q: What small step could help Gargi reconnect with the subject?
qa.a: Choose one topic to read just for fun, like the Cholas under the blanket, with no marks attached, and set a limit on drafts for the seminar paper.

qa.q: What might Neelam be wondering when asking 'Don't you enjoy it at all?'
qa.a: Neelam seems to sense that the work has become all pressure and no pleasure for Gargi, and may be worried about a friend awake at 2 a.m. on a fourth draft.

qa.q: Which page has the font problem?
qa.a: Page 12.

qa.q: What is Chandrika afraid of if there's one mistake?
qa.a: That people will realise Chandrika is 'just normal', so the checking is driven by fear of losing a special image rather than by love of design.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the chat, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Amandeep recalling the fest poster made just for fun; Chandrika saw the difference was grading and agreed to leave page 12 and walk down.

qa.q: How does Amandeep seem to feel about Chandrika's week of rechecking?
qa.a: Amandeep seems worried and caring, seeing the exhaustion under the perfectionism, and uses warmth and a small invitation instead of a lecture.

grounding: A student praised as the best fears one mistake will reveal ordinariness, and the constant checking is driven by fear.
